<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Biointra Renovables Tequila Jalisco, S.A.P.I. de C.V. is not a subsidiary of the Company, and the three LOIs it executed have not been assigned to the Company or BRA. Each LOI remains in effect until the contemplated collaboration is concluded or terminated, and none is a binding commitment. Three of the four LOIs include waste-generation data reported by the counterparty, which, on an annualized basis, aggregate approximately 32,800 cubic meters of vinasse and 4,100 metric tons of bagasse per year. In addition, entities affiliated with our CEO have entered into, or are negotiating, confidentiality agreements with additional tequila producers and spirits groups. Confidentiality agreements do not obligate any party to enter into a commercial transaction. See &#8220;Item 7. Certain Relationships and Related Transactions, and Director Independence.&#8221;</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>Biomass Supply Arrangement</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>On September 24, 2026, Productores Industriales de Biomasa, S.A. de C.V., of Hidalgo del Parral, Chihuahua, executed a Wood Chip and Sawdust Supply, Collection and Delivery Agreement, together with an Incorporation, Precedence and Amendment of Annexes Agreement, under which it would supply wood chips to the Company as an alternative biomass fuel. As of the date of this Amendment, the agreement has not been countersigned by the Company and is not in effect. Its price, moisture and bark parameters remain to be agreed in technical and economic closing certificates, and the annual reference volume of 500,000 metric tons is a planning target rather than a purchase or delivery obligation. No deliveries or payment obligations would arise until the parties sign the technical closing, economic closing and commercial start-up certificates. The agreement provides for a ten-year initial term and may be terminated by either party without cause on 90 days&#8217; notice.</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>Competition</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>The renewable energy and industrial waste-to-energy industries are highly competitive and constantly evolving. We believe our principal competitors for the energy needs of tequila producers are the state-owned electricity utility, Comisi&#243;n Federal de Electricidad (&#8220;CFE&#8221;), and the suppliers of fossil fuels (fuel oil, natural gas and LP gas) used to generate steam and heat. We also expect to compete with independent waste treatment companies, developers and financiers of biogas projects, construction companies expanding into renewable energy and engineering firms offering integrated energy solutions. We intend to compete on price, regulatory compliance, the integration of waste treatment with energy supply, and the absence of up-front investment by the client. Many of our competitors have substantially greater financial, technical and operating resources than we do. See &#8220;Item 1A. Risk Factors.&#8221;</P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>7</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>Government Regulation</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Our planned operations in Mexico are subject to federal, state and municipal laws and regulations governing the management of special waste (including the Integrated Waste Management Law of the State of Jalisco and its regulations), wastewater discharge (including NOM-001-SEMARNAT-2021, administered by the National Water Commission (CONAGUA) and the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (PROFEPA)), environmental impact authorizations, the generation and interconnection of electricity (including the Electricity Sector Law and the rules of the National Energy Commission (CNE) and the Ministry of Energy (SENER)), water concessions and land use. We will need to obtain environmental and construction permits for each operating unit before construction can begin. The regulatory framework for the Mexican electricity sector was substantially reformed in 2024 and 2025, and further changes are possible. See &#8220;Item 1A. Risk Factors &#8212;&nbsp;Risks Related to Our Operations.&#8221;</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>Intellectual Property</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We do not own any patents, registered trademarks or other registered intellectual property. The pelletizing, boiler and biodigestion technologies that we intend to use are available from our technology partners and equipment suppliers, and we have not entered into any license agreement that grants us exclusive rights. We rely on the know-how of our founder and of entities affiliated with him, on confidentiality agreements with counterparties and on the specifications developed with our technology partners.</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>Employees and Human Capital</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We have no employees. Our executive officers devote such time to our business as they consider necessary and currently serve without cash compensation. Administrative, accounting and development activities are carried out by our officers, by outside professional advisors and by personnel of entities affiliated with our Chief Executive Officer, and the cultivation of the BRA properties is carried out through contracted agricultural labor. We expect to hire operating personnel as our first operating units are financed and built.</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>Emerging Growth Company and Smaller Reporting Company Status</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We are an &#8220;emerging growth company,&#8221; as defined in the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act of 2012 (the &#8220;JOBS Act&#8221;), and a &#8220;smaller reporting company,&#8221; as defined in Rule 12b-2 under the Exchange Act. For as long as we remain an emerging growth company we may take advantage of certain exemptions from reporting requirements that apply to other public companies, including an exemption from the auditor attestation requirement of Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, reduced disclosure obligations regarding executive compensation, and exemptions from the requirements to hold non-binding advisory votes on executive compensation. We will remain an emerging growth company until the earliest of (i) the last day of the fiscal year in which our total annual gross revenues exceed $1.235 billion, (ii) the last day of the fiscal year following the fifth anniversary of the first sale of our common equity securities under an effective Securities Act registration statement, (iii) the date on which we have issued more than $1.0 billion in non-convertible debt during the preceding three-year period, and (iv) the date on which we are deemed a &#8220;large accelerated filer.&#8221; We have not elected to opt out of the extended transition period for complying with new or revised financial accounting standards under Section 107 of the JOBS Act, and as a result our financial statements may not be comparable to those of companies that comply with new or revised accounting standards as of public company effective dates. As a smaller reporting company we may also provide scaled disclosure, including two years of audited financial statements and reduced executive compensation disclosure.</P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>8</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P style='font:11pt Times New Roman;margin-top:12pt;margin-bottom:6pt;color:#000000'><B>ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>An investment in our Class A Common Stock involves a high degree of risk. You should carefully consider the risks described below, together with the other information in this Amendment, including our financial statements and the related notes. If any of the following risks occurs, our business, financial condition, results of operations and prospects could be materially and adversely affected, and the trading price of our Class A Common Stock, if a market develops, could decline. Additional risks not presently known to us or that we currently consider immaterial may also impair our business.</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>Summary of Principal Risks</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD>We have no revenue, no operating waste-to-energy facility and no binding customer contracts, and our auditor has expressed substantial doubt about our ability to continue as a going concern.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD>Our four letters of intent are non-binding, and three of them were signed by an entity affiliated with our Chief Executive Officer that is not our subsidiary.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD>We will need approximately $55 million to $62 million of project financing to build our ten planned operating units, and we have no committed source of financing other than uncommitted advances from our Chief Executive Officer.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD>Substantially all of our assets consist of agricultural property in Mexico whose carrying value depends on appraisal-based estimates that our auditor identified as a critical audit matter.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD>Our auditor identified a material weakness in our internal control over financial reporting, and we have no independent directors or audit committee.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD>Our Chief Executive Officer controls approximately 94% of our voting power and, under our Certificate of Incorporation, holds veto rights over board decisions; we will be a &#8220;controlled company&#8221; under Nasdaq rules.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD>Changes in Mexican energy, waste and water regulation, in electricity and fossil fuel prices, and in the value of the Mexican peso could adversely affect our planned business.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD>We do not currently satisfy the initial listing requirements of the Nasdaq Capital Market, and our registration under Section 12(b) will not become effective unless Nasdaq approves our listing; there is no public market for our Class A Common Stock and one may never develop; and sales under the Silver Rock Share Purchase Agreement and related warrants may cause substantial dilution.&nbsp;</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>A. Risks Related to Our Operations</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Existing waste management and renewable energy regulations, and changes to such regulations, may present technical, regulatory and economic barriers to the purchase and use of our waste-to-energy solutions. These barriers could significantly reduce demand for our services or adversely impact the economics of our future energy contracts.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Federal, state and municipal government regulations and policies concerning waste management, renewable energy generation, utility rate structures, interconnection procedures and the internal policies of utilities heavily influence the market for our planned products and services. These regulations and policies often relate to electricity pricing, the treatment and discharge of industrial wastewater and the interconnection of customer-owned renewable energy generation facilities to the national grid. In Mexico, the previous federal administration repeatedly sought to modify these regulations and policies, including those governing special waste such as tequila bagasse and vinasse. Changes of this kind could discourage potential customers from adopting renewable energy solutions, including our planned pellet and biogas systems, and significantly reduce demand for our services. In 2025, the renewable energy landscape in Mexico underwent a profound reconfiguration following the approval of constitutional reforms and the implementation of the Electricity Sector Development Plan (PLADESE) 2025&#8211;2039. The principal risks, classified by their nature, include the following:</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'><B>Legal and regulatory risks.</B> This is the area of greatest uncertainty due to the shift towards a &#8220;binding energy planning&#8221; system.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>CFE&#8217;s dominance.</B> The reform assigns CFE control of 54% of generation, limiting market space for private companies and creating risks of discrimination in energy dispatch.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Discretion in permits.</B> New generation permits and interconnection requests are subject to a &#8220;priority attention&#8221; process (initiated in October 2025). There is a risk that project allocation will not be competitive but will instead be based on strategic criteria of the State.&nbsp;</P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>9</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Uncertainty in self-supply contracts.</B> The review of contracts signed before 2013 and new restrictions on the sale of surplus energy represent a risk of retroactivity and potential international litigation under the USMCA.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Weakening of CELs.</B> The potential disappearance of Clean Energy Certificates as a mandatory mechanism weakens the economic incentives for companies to invest in new renewable plants.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'><B>Technical and infrastructure risks.</B> The Mexican electricity grid faces significant operational stress due to years of insufficient investment in transmission.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Transmission network saturation.</B> Despite the 66 transmission projects announced for 2025&#8211;2026, the current infrastructure remains the bottleneck, causing congestion at key nodes and limiting the evacuation of energy from areas with high solar, wind or biomass generation.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Intermittency and stability.</B> The lack of large-scale storage capacity hinders the integration of additional renewables without jeopardizing the stability of the National Electric System (SEN), which has led to preventive blackouts during periods of high demand.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Lag in decentralization.</B> Although distributed generation continues to grow, the lack of modernization of low- and medium-voltage networks prevents this growth from being orderly and secure for the system.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'><B>Investment and financial risks.</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Public capital constraints.</B> The budget allocated to CFE for 2026 shows a real reduction compared to 2025, leaving an investment gap (estimated at over MXN 100 billion annually) that the public sector cannot cover alone.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Financing costs.</B> Legal uncertainty raises interest rates for projects in Mexico (risk premium), affecting the profitability of clean energy investments.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:4pt;margin-left:27pt'><KBD style='position:absolute;font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-left:-13.5pt'>&#8226;</KBD><B>Barriers to nearshoring.</B> Many multinational companies have sustainability goals that require 100% clean energy. The difficulty in obtaining direct green energy supply contracts jeopardizes the arrival of new industrial investments to the country.&nbsp;</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>In addition, the entry into force of NOM-001-SEMARNAT-2021 represents one of the most significant regulatory challenges for the tequila industry in recent decades. This standard updates the limits for pollutants in wastewater discharges, focusing on the protection of national water bodies. The standard not only tightens the previous limits (NOM-001-1996) but also introduces parameters that were not previously strictly monitored, including stricter limits on biochemical oxygen demand and total suspended solids, new acute toxicity and true color requirements (color being a typical problem with vinasse), a reduction of the maximum discharge temperature from 40&#176;C to 35&#176;C (requiring additional cooling systems, since vinasse leaves the stills at temperatures close to boiling), and sanctions that empower PROFEPA and CONAGUA to impose severe fines or even the closure of wells and production plants. While we believe this standard creates demand for our vinasse treatment solution, it also increases the cost and complexity of the facilities we must build and operate, and any failure of our facilities to comply would expose us to sanctions.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Regulatory limitations associated with technical considerations may limit our ability to sell electricity (but not thermal energy) generated from our waste-to-energy systems in certain regions.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>The generation limits under Mexico&#8217;s current energy policy are central to our planned biogas cogeneration model. Previously, the limit for generating energy without a permit from the Energy Regulatory Commission (CRE) was 0.5 MW. Under the new Electricity Sector Law, this limit has been raised to 0.7 MW, which allows medium-sized businesses and industries to install larger systems without a federal permit; however, the elimination of net metering in favor of less favorable compensation schemes could discourage investment if surplus energy is paid at very low rates. The current government also allows &#8220;self-consumption&#8221; projects of up to 20 MW under a simplified permitting regime, which permits large industries to generate their own energy on a scale that previously required complex generation permits and reduces the load on the national transmission network. The risks of this scheme include the potential overload of saturated distribution networks and the lack of clarity regarding the &#8220;injection rates&#8221; for surpluses, which are still being defined.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>In practice, CFE and the regulatory bodies can impose limits on the amount of electricity that can be fed into the grid from waste-to-energy facilities, or require costly upgrades to substations and power lines before approving interconnection. While certain policies currently allow for expedited or simplified procedures for connecting renewable energy systems to the grid, any modification or elimination of these procedures could negatively impact our ability to sell electricity generated from our planned biogas and cogeneration systems. As the adoption of distributed renewable generation increases, CFE has stated that overgeneration situations could require curtailing renewable resources to maintain grid stability. If our planned facilities were </P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>10</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>curtailed without compensation, or if interconnection limits prevented us from selling electricity, our business, operating results and future growth could be materially and adversely affected. Our planned facilities are each designed to generate less than 20 MW, and the sites we have identified are not located in zones that CFE has designated as overgeneration zones; however, these circumstances could change.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Although our business plan does not depend on government incentives, subsidies and market mechanisms such as Clean Energy Certificates, changes in the availability of these incentives could adversely affect our business.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Federal, state and municipal government bodies in Mexico, as well as regulatory agencies such as the CNE and SENER, provide financial incentives to promote renewable energy adoption. These incentives include tax deductions, subsidies for clean technology deployment, preferential financing programs and market mechanisms such as CELs, which reward generators of renewable electricity with tradable credits. CELs remain mandatory for &#8220;obligated participants&#8221; (large consumers and suppliers); for 2025 the clean energy consumption requirement remained at approximately 13.9%, although proposals exist to raise it gradually to 20%, and a recent Electricity Sector Law initiative proposes that CELs have a validity of two years from issuance. The most significant benefit currently available is the 100% income tax deduction for investment in machinery and equipment for renewable energy generation under Article 34, Section XIII of the Mexican Income Tax Law, and the &#8220;Plan Mexico&#8221; incentives launched in 2025, which include additional deductions of up to 72% on research and related technical training expenses.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We may benefit from these incentives in lowering our cost of capital, encouraging investor participation and reducing the effective price of our planned solutions for industrial clients, and they may enhance the attractiveness of our ESCO model. However, these incentives may expire on a predetermined date, be reduced or terminated as renewable energy adoption increases, or end when allocated funding is exhausted, often without warning and as a result of political or regulatory changes. Any material change in the availability or structure of governmental incentives could have a negative impact on our business, financial condition and growth prospects.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Increases in the cost of biomass feedstock, specialized equipment or tariffs on imported components could adversely impact our business and financial results.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>The low cost and wide availability of biomass feedstock are key assumptions in the pricing of our planned waste-to-energy solutions. A significant increase in the cost of biomass inputs (such as tequila bagasse or vinasse), boilers, pelletizing machinery, anaerobic digesters or other specialized components would impair our ability to compete and our financial results. The cost of raw materials and equipment could increase due to factors beyond our control, supply chain disruptions, or the imposition of tariffs, safeguards or other trade measures on imported machinery. We intend to source pelletizing units, pellet boilers and burners from manufacturers in Mexico and Asia, while control systems (PLCs) typically rely on technology imported from Europe. If tariffs, antidumping duties or countervailing measures are imposed on these imports, the purchase price of our equipment could increase, and our ability to purchase equipment on competitive terms or to access specialized technologies could be limited. Any significant increase in the cost of materials or components could reduce the competitiveness of our solutions, increase our capital requirements and negatively affect our business, financial position and operating results.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>A decrease in the price of electricity generated by CFE or in the cost of fossil fuels could harm our business, financial condition and operating results.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>A client&#8217;s decision to adopt our planned waste-to-energy solutions is expected to be driven primarily by its desire to reduce energy costs while complying with environmental regulations or decarbonization targets. These decisions can also be influenced by the cost of other renewable or conventional energy sources. A decrease in the industrial price of electricity from CFE or in the cost of fossil fuels such as natural gas, fuel oil or LP gas could impair our ability to offer competitive pricing. A direct reduction in industrial electricity tariffs in Mexico appears unlikely in the short term under CFE&#8217;s traditional tariff scheme; in January 2025, large industrial consumers saw increases of between 8% and 12% due to volatility in the price of natural gas, which generates approximately 60% of Mexico&#8217;s electricity, and the depreciation of the peso. A widespread reduction in prices would require consolidation of investment in transmission (the Mexican government has announced a plan of over US$12 billion for 2026 focused on infrastructure), an increased clean energy content in generation (the stated goal is 45% by 2030) and special pricing schemes in industrial corridors to attract nearshoring investment. If industrial electricity prices or fossil fuel costs decrease for any reason, the purchase of our pellets, biogas or cogeneration services would become less economically attractive, we might be unable to attract customers, and we might experience defaults under any contracts we enter into.</P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>11</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Industrial customers are expected to represent substantially all of our business, and the industrial energy market is sensitive to price fluctuations.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Industrial and commercial customers in Mexico typically pay higher rates for electricity and fossil fuels than residential customers. Because the price we expect to charge industrial customers for our biofuels must be lower than their current retail rate, any significant decrease in the retail price of electricity or fossil fuels for industrial users could have a significant impact on our ability to attract and retain customers. Although we believe that the principal challenge faced by tequila producers is the treatment of their special waste, and that it is improbable that the Mexican government will subsidize electricity or conventional fuels for industry, if that were to happen our business would be negatively impacted.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We may not realize the anticipated benefits of future acquisitions, and the integration of acquisitions may disrupt our business.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>In the future, we may acquire renewable energy companies, project pipelines, waste-to-energy facilities or proprietary technologies, or enter into joint ventures and other strategic initiatives. Our ability to integrate acquisitions is unproven. Any acquisition carries numerous risks, including difficulty in assimilating operations and personnel, challenges in integrating acquired technologies or processes with our planned pelletization, biogas or cogeneration systems, difficulty in maintaining internal controls and compliance policies during the transition, disruption of ongoing business and diversion of management attention, difficulty integrating accounting and management information systems, the inability to retain key personnel, customers, suppliers and local partners, failure to achieve financial and strategic goals, acquisition-related costs and amortization of intangible assets, failure of due diligence to identify environmental liabilities, regulatory noncompliance or hidden financial obligations, the inability to assert that internal controls over financial reporting are effective following integration, and delays in obtaining required governmental approvals, including environmental permits, interconnection approvals or waste treatment licenses. If we are unable to integrate future acquisitions successfully, or if anticipated benefits are not realized, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be materially and adversely affected.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We face competition from both traditional energy companies and renewable energy companies.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>The renewable energy and industrial waste-to-energy industries are highly competitive and constantly evolving. We believe our main competitors are CFE and the fossil fuel suppliers that provide electricity, steam and heat to our potential customers, with whom we would compete primarily on price, regulatory compliance and ease of adoption. We also expect to face competition from other participants in the value chain, including financial organizations that fund the development of biogas projects, independent waste treatment companies, large construction companies expanding into renewable energy and engineering firms offering comprehensive energy solutions. Competitors have increasingly begun vertically integrating their operations to offer comprehensive products and services similar to those we plan to offer, and consolidation among renewable energy providers is increasing. If we are unable to differentiate our offerings, maintain competitive pricing or establish a market presence, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be materially and adversely affected.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We will depend on a limited number of suppliers of specialized equipment and on a limited number of waste generators for biomass inputs. Any shortage, delay or price change could result in project delays, cancellations and the loss of our ability to compete.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We intend to purchase pelletization machinery, biogas digesters, boilers, control systems and other specialized components from a limited number of suppliers, and to source biomass inputs such as tequila bagasse and vinasse from a limited number of industrial producers. This reliance will make us susceptible to quality issues, shortages and price fluctuations. If we fail to develop, maintain and expand our relationships with equipment suppliers and biomass providers, we may be unable to meet anticipated demand, or may only be able to offer our services at higher costs or after delays. If one or more of the suppliers or waste generators we rely upon ceases or reduces production, we may be unable to identify alternate suppliers or qualify alternative technologies on commercially reasonable terms. Many of our suppliers may be single-source providers of critical components, and qualifying alternate suppliers may be time-consuming and costly and may force us to modify our process designs. Our need to purchase equipment globally also subjects us to currency risk: any decline in the exchange rate of the U.S. dollar or the Mexican peso against the functional currency of our component suppliers could increase our equipment costs. Changes in economic and business conditions, wars, governmental changes and other factors beyond our control could also affect our suppliers&#8217; solvency and ability to deliver components on a timely basis.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Our agricultural operations are subject to weather, pest, disease, yield and water risks.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>The bearer plants on the BRA properties consist of avocado trees and blue agave. Agricultural yields are subject to weather conditions, pests, plant disease, water availability and market prices for avocado and agave, each of which is outside our control. The water concession that supports irrigation of the properties has an initial term of ten years, is subject to renewal and to </P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>12</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>compliance with Mexican water law, and the transfer of the concession to BRA must be registered with CONAGUA. If yields decline, if the concession is not renewed or if the properties&#8217; productive capacity is impaired, we could be required to record impairment charges, and the properties may not generate the agricultural cash flows we anticipate.</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>B. Risks Related to Our Company</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We have no revenue, have identified substantial doubt about our ability to continue as a going concern, and do not expect waste-to-energy revenue in 2026.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We have not generated revenue since inception. As of June 30, 2026, we had cash of $15,602, a working capital of $864,087, amounts due to a company controlled by our Chief Executive Officer of $35,441 and an accumulated deficit of $1,785,401, and we incurred a net loss of $488,324 for the six months ended June 30, 2026. Our independent registered public accounting firm included an explanatory paragraph in its report on our financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025 regarding substantial doubt about our ability to continue as a going concern. Under our current development plan, construction of our first operating units is not expected to begin until 2027, and management&#8217;s modeled capital expenditure for the ten planned operating units is approximately $55 million to $62 million. We will require substantial additional financing, which may not be available on acceptable terms or at all. If we cannot obtain financing, we may be required to reduce, delay or cease our development activities.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Our letters of intent are non-binding, and three of our four letters of intent were signed by an entity that is not our subsidiary; we have no binding customer contracts.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Our commercial pipeline consists of four non-binding letters of intent with tequila and agave producers. Three were executed in 2024 by Biointra Renovables Tequila Jalisco, S.A.P.I. de C.V., which is affiliated with our Chief Executive Officer and is not our subsidiary. Only one LOI was executed by our subsidiary BRA. The LOIs contain no price, volume or term-of-service commitments and may be terminated at any time without liability. If we are unable to convert these relationships into binding, enforceable waste-treatment and energy-supply contracts on acceptable terms, we may be unable to obtain project financing or generate revenue, and our business would be materially and adversely affected.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We have a limited operating history, and our business plan is unproven.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We were incorporated in May 2024 and have not built or operated a waste-to-energy facility. Our business plan relies on technologies and processes that have been demonstrated by our technology partners and affiliates on a limited scale but have not been operated by us at commercial scale, on obtaining environmental and construction permits that we have not yet obtained, on supplier quotations that require updating, and on customer relationships that are not yet contractual. Our estimates of construction timing, capital expenditure, operating costs and treatment fees may prove to be inaccurate, and we may be unable to execute our business plan.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>The carrying value of our agricultural property depends on significant estimates, and we are exposed to agricultural, title and water-rights risks.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Substantially all of our assets consist of agricultural property recorded at a fair value of $5,426,066 at acquisition (carrying amount of $857,121 for inventory, $4,120,680 for property and equipment and $40,472 for water licenses at June 30, 2026), determined from third-party appraisals that rely on market comparables, replacement-cost inputs, crop valuation inputs and water-right valuation inputs. Our auditor identified this valuation as a critical audit matter. If the estimates underlying the valuation prove inaccurate, if title or registration defects are identified in the Mexican public property registry, if the water concession transfer is not registered with CONAGUA, or if the properties&#8217; productive capacity declines, we could be required to record impairment charges. Bearer plants and land improvements are being depreciated over four years, which will result in significant non-cash depreciation charges in 2026 and 2027.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We are exposed to fluctuations in the Mexican peso.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>The functional currency of BRA is the Mexican peso, while our reporting currency is the U.S. dollar. During 2025 we recorded a foreign currency translation gain of $95,430 and during the six months ended June 30, 2026 a further gain of $153,937 in other comprehensive income, reflecting the appreciation of the peso against the dollar; these gains could reverse. Our planned capital expenditures are largely denominated in U.S. dollars and euros, while our expected revenues are denominated in Mexican pesos. A depreciation of the peso could materially reduce the U.S. dollar value of our assets and future revenue and increase our costs.</P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>13</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We depend on advances from our Chief Executive Officer and entities he controls, which are not committed.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Since inception, our operations have been funded principally by advances from a company controlled by our Chief Executive Officer and by Mr. Lahud personally. These advances are undocumented, unsecured, non-interest-bearing and due on demand, and totaled $35,441 at June 30, 2026. Mr. Lahud and his affiliates are under no obligation to continue to fund us, and a demand for repayment would exhaust our cash. If related-party funding ceases before we obtain third-party financing, we may be unable to pay our professional advisors, complete our listing process or continue operations.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We may need additional funding to execute our business plan and fund operations, and such funding may not be available on reasonable terms or at all.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We will require significant additional capital within the next 12 months and beyond. We intend to raise funds through the sale of equity and debt securities, project financing and commercial debt financing, but there can be no guarantee that such funds will be available on commercially reasonable terms, if at all. If financing is not available on satisfactory terms, we may be unable to expand or continue our business as planned. Any debt financing we obtain will increase expenses, must be repaid regardless of operating results and may involve restrictive covenants. If we issue equity securities, the percentage ownership of existing stockholders will be reduced and stockholders may experience dilution in net book value per share. Our ability to obtain financing may be impaired by conditions in the capital markets, investor sentiment toward renewable energy and waste-to-energy projects, the going-concern explanatory paragraph in our auditor&#8217;s report and the fact that we are not yet profitable.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We may be negatively affected by adverse general economic conditions.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Conditions in the Mexican, United States and global economies remain uncertain. Softening markets, inflationary pressures, reduced industrial demand, wavering investor confidence, geopolitical instability, trade disputes, terrorism or war could reduce industrial customers&#8217; willingness or ability to invest in renewable energy solutions, delay project development, limit our access to financing or increase our cost of capital. Currency fluctuations between the U.S. dollar and the Mexican peso could further impact our operating costs and revenues.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Our principal stockholder controls our activities and holds veto rights under our Certificate of Incorporation, which may prevent us from taking actions that other stockholders might view favorably.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Mr. Ra&#250;l Lahud Quiroz, holds 105,039,427 shares of Class A Common Stock and all 10,000,000 outstanding shares of Class B Common Stock, which carry twenty votes per share. As of the date of this Amendment, these holdings represent approximately 84.9% of our outstanding Class A Common Stock and approximately 94.2% of the combined voting power of our outstanding common stock. In addition, Article III.E of our Certificate of Incorporation provides that the holder of the Class B Common Stock is entitled to maintain veto power over any vote of our board of directors and that the individual representing the Class B Common Stock may effectively make board decisions on his own, including the hiring of executive officers. As a result, Mr. Lahud controls all matters requiring stockholder or board approval, including the election of directors and the approval of significant corporate transactions, mergers, acquisitions and related-party transactions. This concentration of ownership and control could delay, deter or prevent a change in control that other stockholders might view as favorable, limits the ability of minority stockholders to influence corporate matters and could result in decisions that prioritize Mr. Lahud&#8217;s interests over those of other investors.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We will be a &#8220;controlled company&#8221; under Nasdaq rules, and we have no independent directors and no audit committee.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Because Mr. Lahud holds more than 50% of our voting power, upon listing we will be a &#8220;controlled company&#8221; within the meaning of the Nasdaq listing rules and may elect not to comply with certain corporate governance requirements, including the requirements that a majority of the board of directors consist of independent directors and that we have independent compensation and nominating committees. Our board of directors currently has no independent members and no standing committees. To list on Nasdaq we will be required to establish an audit committee composed of independent directors meeting the requirements of Rule 10A-3 under the Exchange Act, and we have not yet identified qualified independent directors. Until we do so, our stockholders will not have the protections afforded by independent board oversight of our financial reporting, executive compensation and related-party transactions.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Our directors and officers have conflicts of interest, and we have no written related-party transaction policy.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Our directors and officers are, or may become, officers, directors, controlling stockholders or partners of other entities, including LAHUD150, S.A. de C.V. and Biointra Renovables Tequila Jalisco, S.A.P.I. de C.V., which are affiliated with Mr. Lahud but are not our subsidiaries. Biointra Renovables Tequila Jalisco, S.A.P.I. de C.V. executed three of our four letters of intent. Potential conflicts of interest exist regarding the allocation of time, business opportunities and the assignment of these relationships to the Company. We have not adopted a written policy for the review and approval of related-party transactions, </P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>14</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>and our Certificate of Incorporation and Bylaws do not require officers and directors to present business opportunities to the Company. Our officers devote such time to our business as they believe necessary and are not required to devote their full time to us.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We may depend upon outside advisors, who may not be available on reasonable terms or when needed.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>To supplement the experience of our officers and directors, we rely on accountants, technical experts, appraisers, attorneys and other consultants. The selection of such advisors is made by our board of directors without input from stockholders, and these advisors are retained on an as-needed basis without continuing fiduciary obligations to us. There can be no assurance that qualified advisors will be available on commercially reasonable terms when their services are required. In certain cases we may engage affiliates to provide advisory services, which could create conflicts of interest. Failure to secure appropriate outside advisors could impair our ability to execute our business plan, maintain regulatory compliance and respond to technical and financial challenges.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Our auditor identified a material weakness in our internal control over financial reporting, and if we fail to remediate it or identify additional material weaknesses, the accuracy and timeliness of our financial reporting may be adversely affected.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>In connection with the audit of our consolidated financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, our independent registered public accounting firm identified a material weakness in our internal control over financial reporting, consisting of the absence of effective policies and procedures to provide adequate, independent oversight over financial reporting, the timely preparation, review and approval of accounting records and journal entries, and a lack of segregation of duties, resulting from our small size and limited accounting personnel. A material weakness is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in internal control over financial reporting such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of our annual or interim financial statements will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis. Management is evaluating and implementing improvements to our financial reporting and review process, including the engagement of an outside accounting firm to prepare our financial statements, but the material weakness had not been remediated as of the date of this Amendment, and remediation will depend on our ability to hire qualified accounting personnel and to establish independent oversight.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>If we are not able to maintain effective internal control over financial reporting and disclosure controls and procedures, or if additional material weaknesses are discovered in future periods, a risk that is heightened by the complexity of our planned operations, regulatory compliance requirements in Mexico, the use of two functional currencies and the need to consolidate financial data across entities, we may be unable to accurately and timely report our financial position, results of operations or cash flows. This could result in late filings of our periodic reports, restatements of our financial statements or other corrective disclosures, and could impair our ability to raise capital or meet investor expectations.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Reporting requirements under the Exchange Act and compliance with the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 are costly and may increase substantially.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Once the registration of our Class A Common Stock becomes effective, we will be required to file annual, quarterly and current reports with the SEC and to comply with the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the Dodd-Frank Act and the Nasdaq listing rules, which will require us to engage legal, accounting, auditing and other professional services. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires, among other things, that we design, implement and maintain adequate internal controls over financial reporting. The costs of compliance, combined with our limited technically qualified personnel, may make it difficult for us to design, implement and maintain adequate internal controls. We are working with our legal, accounting and financial advisors to identify areas in which changes should be made to our financial and management control systems, including corporate governance, disclosure controls and procedures, and financial reporting and accounting systems. We estimate that the aggregate cost of increased legal services, accounting and audit functions, personnel such as a chief financial officer familiar with public company reporting, consultants to design and implement internal controls, and financial printing will be at least several hundred thousand dollars per year. If and when we retain independent directors or additional members of senior management, we will incur additional expenses for director compensation and directors&#8217; and officers&#8217; liability insurance, which we cannot estimate at this time. These expenses, individually or in the aggregate, may be material, and being a public company may make it more difficult or costly to obtain certain types of insurance and to attract and retain qualified directors and officers. If compliance requirements divert management&#8217;s attention from developing our waste-to-energy projects, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be materially and adversely affected.</P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>15</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We are an emerging growth company, and the reduced disclosure requirements applicable to emerging growth companies may make our Class A Common Stock less attractive to investors.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>For as long as we remain an emerging growth company, we may take advantage of exemptions from various reporting requirements, including exemption from the auditor attestation requirements of Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and reduced executive compensation disclosure, and we have not opted out of the extended transition period for complying with new or revised accounting standards. We cannot predict whether investors will find our Class A Common Stock less attractive as a result, which could result in a less active trading market and greater volatility in the price of our shares.</P>
<P style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:9pt;margin-bottom:5pt;color:#000000'><B>C. Risks Related to Our Securities</B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We do not currently satisfy the initial listing requirements of the Nasdaq Capital Market, and the registration of our Class A Common Stock under Section 12(b) of the Exchange Act will not become effective unless Nasdaq approves our listing application.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We have filed this registration statement in connection with our planned listing on the Nasdaq Capital Market. Under Section 12(d) of the Exchange Act, our registration will become effective only after Nasdaq certifies to the SEC that our Class A Common Stock has been approved for listing. Based on our stockholder base and our financial condition as of the date of this Amendment, we do not qualify for initial listing on the Nasdaq Capital Market. The Nasdaq Capital Market initial listing standards require, among other things, a minimum bid price of $4.00 per share; at least 1,000,000 unrestricted publicly held shares with a market value of at least $15 million; at least 300 round-lot holders, at least 50% of whom must each hold unrestricted shares with a market value of at least $2,500; stockholders&#8217; equity of at least $5 million (together with a two-year operating history), a market value of listed securities of at least $50 million, or net income of at least $750,000; and compliance with Nasdaq&#8217;s corporate governance requirements, including an audit committee of independent directors. We have no revenue and an accumulated deficit, our stockholders&#8217; equity was $5,025,239 at June 30, 2026 and will decline as we incur further losses unless we raise capital, we have no operating history of two years in the sense contemplated by the rules, and we have no independent directors. As to the stockholder base, 287 of our 306 holders of record currently hold unrestricted shares, and we expect that number to exceed 300 in December 2026 when the Rule 144 holding period for the shares sold in our Regulation S offering in November and December 2025 expires (see &#8220;Item 9 &#8212;&nbsp;Shares Eligible for Future Sale&#8221;); however, approximately 270 of those holders hold 400 shares each, so that at the $4.00 minimum bid price fewer than half of them would hold unrestricted shares with a market value of $2,500, and our unrestricted publicly held shares would have a market value well below $15 million. To qualify for listing we will need to raise additional equity capital, broaden our stockholder base so that a sufficient number of round-lot holders hold unrestricted shares with the required market value, appoint independent directors and establish an audit committee, and satisfy Nasdaq that our shares will trade at or above the minimum bid price. We may be unable to do any of these things, and Nasdaq also has broad discretion to deny listing on the basis of public interest concerns, including concerns about related-party transactions, the concentration of control or the source of a company&#8217;s assets. If Nasdaq does not approve our listing, our registration under Section 12(b) will not become effective, we will not become a reporting company by means of this registration statement, no public market for our Class A Common Stock will develop through Nasdaq, and the Silver Rock Share Purchase Agreement, which is conditioned on a public listing, will not become available to us.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>There has been no public market for our Class A Common Stock, and an active, liquid and orderly trading market may not develop or be sustained.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Prior to a listing, there has been no public market for our Class A Common Stock. If our Class A Common Stock is listed on Nasdaq without an underwritten offering, the initial trading price will be determined by buy and sell orders collected by Nasdaq from broker-dealers rather than by negotiation with underwriters, and there may initially be either a lack of supply of, or a lack of demand for, our shares. We have not consulted with existing stockholders regarding their desire or plans to sell shares in the public market following a listing, nor have we discussed with potential investors their intentions to purchase our shares. In the case of a lack of supply, the trading price may rise to unsustainable levels; in the case of a lack of demand, the trading price could decline significantly and rapidly. Institutional investors may be discouraged from purchasing our shares if they are unable to acquire sufficient blocks in the open market, and without the stabilizing presence of long-term institutional holders the market for our securities may be more volatile. An active, liquid and orderly trading market may not develop or be sustained, which could depress the trading price of our Class A Common Stock and impair your ability to sell your shares.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>The price of our Class A Common Stock could be highly volatile.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>If a market develops, our Class A Common Stock may be subject to significant price volatility, low trading volumes and wide spreads between bid and ask prices. Due to the limited volume of shares that may trade on any given day, persons buying or </P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>16</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>selling in relatively small quantities may easily influence the price of our shares, and large percentage changes could occur during a single trading session. Holders of our Class A Common Stock may be unable to liquidate their investment readily and may be forced to sell at depressed prices. Broad market fluctuations, general economic and political conditions in Mexico and the United States, regulatory developments, our failure to meet development milestones and sales by our stockholders may also adversely affect the market price of our Class A Common Stock.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>If our Class A Common Stock is not listed on a national securities exchange, it may be subject to the SEC&#8217;s penny stock rules, which could limit its tradability.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>If our Class A Common Stock is not approved for listing on Nasdaq and instead becomes quoted on an over-the-counter market at a price below $5.00 per share, it would likely be a &#8220;penny stock&#8221; under Rule 3a51-1 under the Exchange Act. Broker-dealers effecting transactions in penny stocks must comply with Rule 15g-9 and related rules, which require, among other things, delivery of a standardized risk disclosure document, disclosure of commissions and current quotations, and a written determination that the penny stock is a suitable investment for the purchaser. These requirements reduce the level of trading activity in the secondary market for penny stocks and could make it more difficult for holders to sell their shares.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Sales of our Class A Common Stock to Silver Rock Group under the Share Purchase Agreement, and the issuance and exercise of the related warrants, may cause substantial dilution.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Under our Share Purchase Agreement dated August 29, 2024 with Silver Rock Group (&#8220;Silver Rock&#8221;), we may sell up to $350,000,000 of Class A Common Stock to Silver Rock over the 36 months following our public listing, in tranches of up to one million shares at a price equal to a 10% discount to the lowest trading price during the ten trading days preceding each draw-down notice, subject to volume limitations. Upon our public listing, we are also required to issue to Silver Rock five-year warrants to purchase a number of shares equal to 4% of our fully diluted outstanding shares, at an exercise price equal to the lower of $2.00 per share or 110% of the listing price. We issued 2,178,656 shares of Class A Common Stock to Silver Rock as a commitment fee in the first quarter of 2026. On November 2, 2026, we and Silver Rock entered into Amendment No. 1 to the Share Purchase Agreement, which confirms the $350,000,000 aggregate purchase commitment, provides that the warrant exercise price will be fixed on the listing date and will not thereafter be reset by reference to the market price, limits the number of shares that may be registered for resale by Silver Rock under any single registration statement to 29.99% of our then-outstanding shares, provides that we will not issue shares to Silver Rock under the agreement and the warrants (including the commitment shares) in excess of 19.99% of our shares outstanding immediately prior to our listing unless stockholder approval is obtained, and makes the agreement non-exclusive. Mr. Lahud, as the holder of a majority of our voting power, is able to provide that stockholder approval. Draw-downs under the agreement and exercises of the warrants would be made at prices below the prevailing market price and may cause substantial dilution to existing stockholders and depress the trading price of our Class A Common Stock. Sales under the agreement will also require the registration of the resale of those shares under the Securities Act or an available exemption.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>Future sales of our Class A Common Stock, including sales of shares that are already freely tradable and sales of restricted securities under Rule 144, may have a depressive effect on our stock price.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>Of our 123,650,883 outstanding shares of Class A Common Stock as of November 4, 2026, 14,924,800 shares held by 287 non-affiliates are no longer subject to Securities Act restrictive legends, following their removal by our transfer agent on May 11, 2026 in reliance on the Rule 144 opinion of our counsel filed as Exhibit 99.3 (see &#8220;Item 9 &#8212;&nbsp;Shares Eligible for Future Sale&#8221;), and could be sold immediately upon a listing; a further 8,000 shares held by seventeen holders will become freely tradable in November and December 2026. None of our stockholders has entered into a lock-up agreement. The remaining 108,726,083 shares, including the 105,039,427 shares held by our Chief Executive Officer, are &#8220;restricted securities&#8221; within the meaning of Rule 144 under the Securities Act or are held by an affiliate, and may be resold only pursuant to an effective registration statement or an exemption from registration. In general, under Rule 144 as currently in effect, once we have been subject to Exchange Act reporting for at least 90 days, a non-affiliate who has held restricted securities for at least six months may sell them without limitation, and an affiliate who has held restricted securities for at least six months may sell within any three-month period a number of shares that does not exceed the greater of 1% of the outstanding shares of the class or the average weekly trading volume during the four calendar weeks preceding the sale, subject to manner-of-sale, notice and current public information requirements. We also intend to register the resale of certain restricted shares on Form S-1. Sales of a substantial number of shares, or the perception that such sales may occur, could depress the price of our Class A Common Stock in any market that may develop.</P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=center style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin:0'><FONT style=font-size:9pt>17</FONT></P>
<HR style='page-break-after:always;border:0;height:3pt;background-color:#0000A0;margin:8pt 0'><P style=line-height:0;margin:0></P>
<HR style='border:0;height:0;width:0;margin:14pt 0 0 0'><P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>If the registration of our Class A Common Stock is revoked or we fail to maintain our Nasdaq listing, our business opportunities may diminish.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>If, after our registration becomes effective, we fail to comply with our reporting obligations, the SEC could suspend trading in or revoke the registration of our Class A Common Stock, and if we fail to satisfy Nasdaq&#8217;s continued listing standards our shares could be delisted. In either case we would lose the ability to access the capital markets in the same manner as a listed reporting company, which would impair our ability to raise capital through the issuance of shares, reduce investor confidence, limit liquidity in our Class A Common Stock and restrict our ability to pursue growth opportunities.</P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:7pt;margin-bottom:4pt;color:#000000'><B><I>We do not anticipate paying cash dividends on our common stock.</I></B></P>
<P align=justify style='font:10pt Times New Roman;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:6pt'>We have never paid cash dividends and do not anticipate paying any cash dividends in the foreseeable future. Any future determination to pay dividends will be at the discretion of our board of directors and will depend upon our financial condition, results of operations, capital requirements, contractual restrictions and other factors the board deems relevant. As a result, investors may need to rely on sales of their shares after price appreciation, if any, as the only means of realizing a return on their investment.</P>
